posts.title: A Concurrency Group Is a Discard Policy
posts.summary: A concurrency group is not merely a resource limit. It defines whether later work replaces earlier work, whether an in-progress operation can be interrupted, and which commit never receives a result.

posts.title: A Database Backup Is Not a Restore Test
posts.summary: Test restoration on a schedule, verify application-level invariants afterward, and measure recovery time. A green backup job is not evidence of recoverability.

posts.title: An Environment Variable Is a Deployment-Time API
posts.summary: Parse configuration once at startup, validate it into a named schema, and surface the effective non-secret settings. Deployment configuration deserves an API contract.

posts.title: An Empty Search Result Is Not Evidence That Nothing Exists
posts.summary: `[]` can mean no matches, an incomplete index, a permission boundary, a truncated search, or a query against yesterday's snapshot. Make a tool state which of those it means before an agent tells a user that no record exists.

posts.title: A Date Is Not a Timestamp
posts.summary: Keep civil dates, local date-times, and instants as different types. A bare YYYY-MM-DD should not pass through a timestamp parser merely because both happen to use ISO-looking text.

posts.title: Starting a Job Is Not the Same as Finishing It
posts.summary: A successful call can mean that work was accepted, not that its external effect happened. Model long-running work as an operation with a durable status and make agents distinguish started from completed.

posts.title: Test the Invariant, Not the Happy Path
posts.summary: Find the rule that must always hold, then generate or enumerate cases around it. Happy-path examples show a feature works once; invariants show it keeps working.

posts.title: Authorize the Next Action, Not the Whole Agent
posts.summary: Represent authorization as a scoped, expiring capability for the concrete next action. It is easier to review, revoke, and audit than a permanent agent role.

posts.title: An API Deprecation Needs a Removal Test
posts.summary: Deprecations finish when the old behavior can be removed safely. Add contract checks and usage evidence that exercise that future state before the deadline.

posts.title: Test Data Is Production Configuration
posts.summary: Version, review, and deliberately compose test data. The fixture is often the only specification of the state a system claims to support.

posts.title: A Tool Error Is an Instruction to Your Agent
posts.summary: Tool errors are part of an agent's control loop. Return a bounded, typed recovery signal so the agent can distinguish a repairable request from a policy denial, a rate limit, and an action whose completion is unknown.

posts.title: A Feature Flag Does Not Undo an Irrevocable Change
posts.summary: Use flags to limit exposure, but design a compensating action for every irreversible side effect. A toggle is not a rollback plan.

posts.title: Retry Queues Need Deadlines, Not Just Attempt Counts
posts.summary: Attach an expiry to retryable work. The deadline protects systems from turning a temporary dependency failure into stale, surprising side effects.

posts.title: A Log Line Cannot Prove a Message Was Processed
posts.summary: Define processing by its durable effect and acknowledgement boundary, not by an optimistic log line emitted at the start of a handler.

posts.title: A Test Environment That Skips Auth Is Not Staging
posts.summary: Use test identities and realistic authorization paths in staging. A bypassed auth layer makes a fast demo environment, not a production rehearsal.

posts.title: Schema Validation Does Not Prove a Migration Is Safe
posts.summary: Schema validation catches shape errors, not semantic compatibility. Test migrations against representative old data and the decisions consumers make from it.

posts.title: A Valid JSON Response Can Still Be a Bad Answer
posts.summary: A response schema proves the shape of an answer, not whether an answer should be given. Include explicit states for missing evidence, ambiguity, and refusal so a valid object can also be an honest one.

posts.title: Prompt Caching Makes Prompt Layout a Production Interface
posts.summary: A prompt cache reuses an exact rendered prefix, not an abstract idea of a similar prompt. Structure stable context deliberately, put volatile work at the tail, and measure cache changes like any other production interface change.

posts.title: Agent Tool Calls Need Traces, Not Just Logs
posts.summary: Tool logs answer what ran. A trace answers which agent decision caused it, what it waited on, and whether the failure belongs to the model, orchestration, or downstream service.

posts.title: The Memory-Baseline Floor Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: A stale workspace is not permission to forget a newer verified state. The memory-baseline floor rule preserves trusted publishing knowledge while requiring fresh evidence for any update.

posts.title: The Three-Anchor Baseline Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: One latest version is rarely enough for automated publishing. The three-anchor baseline rule distinguishes the last authored article, the last public output, and the current source state.

posts.title: The Draft-Only Source-Advance Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Draft creation changes the authoring baseline, not necessarily the public site. The draft-only source-advance rule preserves both facts without treating an unpublished placeholder as a release.

posts.title: The Remote-Draft-Tail Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Clean is not current. The remote-draft-tail rule requires an authoring run to absorb or account for newly created drafts before it produces the next publication.

posts.title: The Scheduled-Window Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Schedules describe intent, not an exact execution guarantee. The scheduled-window rule uses measured delivery windows and explicit escalation thresholds for reliable publishing automation.

posts.title: The Branch-Name Catch-Up Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: The branch-name catch-up rule separates published content from local reference hygiene. After a successful side-path release, update the durable working baseline so future automation starts from the truth.

posts.title: The Rejoin-Before-Rebind Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: An isolated copy is not automatically orphaned work. The rejoin-before-rebind rule checks for already-integrated content before creating duplicate recovery branches or releases.

posts.title: The Semantic-No-Op Advance Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: A new version is not always a new story. The semantic-no-op advance rule updates operational baselines while reserving editorial announcements for reader-visible change.

posts.title: The Merge-Base Deletion Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: An absent page is not automatically a deletion. The merge-base deletion rule asks whether a source actually removed content or merely lacks a change introduced elsewhere.

posts.title: The Publish-Surface Novelty Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Not every repository change is a publishing change. The publish-surface novelty rule separates reader-visible updates from operational churn so automation does not manufacture a false content backlog.

posts.title: The Same-Tree Dedup Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: A new event is not necessarily new content. The same-tree dedup rule groups equivalent candidates before ranking or publishing them, reducing duplicate releases and noisy review.

posts.title: The Authority-Scoped Convergence Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: There is no such thing as globally converged publishing state. The authority-scoped convergence rule requires every claim of alignment to name the source that grants release permission.

posts.title: The Cache Key Is a Privacy Boundary
posts.summary: Treat cache-key design as authorization design: every input that changes a permitted response must be represented or the response must not be shared.

posts.title: The One-Step Catch-Up Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Progress is not convergence. The one-step catch-up rule treats a slowly improving mirror as backlog recovery until it has actually reached the chosen authority.

posts.title: The Snapshot-Anchor Lag Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Freshness has two dimensions: when a snapshot was made and what editorial state it inherited. The snapshot-anchor lag rule keeps a new timestamp from overruling an older source baseline.

posts.title: The Refreshed-Remote Role Check for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: A reachable remote tip is not automatically the right publish candidate. Candidate election should classify branch role and content type before following a freshly fetched head.

posts.title: The Lineage-Over-Timestamp Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: When a later unbranched snapshot forks from an older commit and drops newer published posts, publish selection must prefer authoritative lineage over raw recency.

posts.title: The Snapshot-Stream Identity Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Repeated worktree snapshot commits with the same generator pattern should be tracked as a named side stream outside the publish branch. That preserves evidence and keeps backlog, freshness, and reconciliation logic attached to the authoritative lineage.

posts.title: The Snapshot-Commit Quarantine Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should not count every local content-bearing commit as release backlog. Snapshot commits on side refs need their own quarantined state until they land on the elected publishing lineage.

posts.title: The Baseline-Anchored Backlog Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should record backlog against a specific shared baseline commit and date. That preserves useful local queue accounting during remote uncertainty without pretending stale divergence numbers describe the live remote branch.

posts.title: Background Work Needs a Named Owner
posts.summary: Every background task needs a durable identity, a responsible service, a deadline, and a terminal outcome that another system can inspect.

posts.title: The Contradicted-Baseline Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should rank branch evidence by freshness, mark contradicted baselines explicitly, and keep that contradiction sticky until a new successful fetch establishes a verified remote baseline.

posts.title: The Divergence-Confidence Label for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should label divergence evidence before acting on it. Verified counts may drive push and rejoin decisions, cached counts may drive backlog accounting in degraded mode, and unknown counts should block claims that depend on current remote truth.

posts.title: The Backlog-Rejoin Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should treat the first successful contact with the remote after a local-only backlog as a rejoin event, not as permission to push blindly. A backlog-rejoin gate fetches the live branch, measures divergence, merges or replays canonical source intent, rebuilds from the remote-inclusive baseline, and returns to normal publish mode only after the queue is collapsed.

posts.title: The Unpublished Backlog Budget for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should treat repeated local-only success as a queue with a budget, not as indefinite progress. An unpublished backlog budget tracks how many publish-ready commits are stranded ahead of the last verified remote baseline, adds age and blast-radius limits, and escalates before the public site falls quietly behind.

posts.title: The Prior-Run Memory Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets safer when each run begins by reading a compact memory of the last verified workspace, build surface, blocked external actions, and local recovery state. A prior-run memory gate turns yesterday's evidence into today's preflight instead of forcing the agent to rediscover the same environment failures.

posts.title: The Instruction-Runtime Parity Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should treat instruction-referenced commands and helpers as part of the executable environment, not as prose. An instruction-runtime parity rule checks those assumptions up front, defines explicit fallback policy, and refuses silent improvisation when runtime reality does not match the workflow contract.

posts.title: Repository Context Is a Dependency, Not a Prompt Attachment
posts.summary: Give coding agents a deliberate repository slice: the relevant code, tests, policy files, and current Git state. More files are not automatically more context.

posts.title: The Attachment-Bias Check for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should not prefer an attached checkout just because it looks tidier in `git status`. An attachment-bias check compares candidate workspaces by verified post corpus and commit freshness first, then repairs branch attachment on the winning candidate instead of regressing to older attached history.

posts.title: A Screenshot Cannot Test the Interaction That Produced It
posts.summary: Use screenshots for visual assertions and browser interaction tests for behavior. A static image cannot validate the path a user took to reach it.

posts.title: Secret Rotation Is an Availability Exercise
posts.summary: Design rotation as a staged compatibility change: introduce, distribute, verify adoption, then retire. Replacing a secret in one step is an outage strategy.

posts.title: The Recovery-Pointer Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should not rely on memory or filesystem archaeology to recover a blocked-but-buildable release. A recovery-pointer rule records the exact local candidate path, commit, and latest post so the next run can resume from verified state instead of a stale checkout.

posts.title: The File Name Is Not the File Type
posts.summary: Classify uploads from validated content, keep them outside executable paths, and serve them with deliberate content-disposition and type policies.

posts.title: Rate Limits Need a Budget the Client Can See
posts.summary: Expose a rate-limit policy and remaining budget deliberately. Clients can then schedule work instead of discovering capacity only by being rejected.

posts.title: The Push-Path Reachability Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should stop pretending a successful local build equals a successful release. A push-path reachability gate verifies DNS, transport, and remote ref access early, then downgrades unreachable remotes from 'publish failed' to 'publish blocked by environment.'

posts.title: The Verified-Local-Lineage Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing loses continuity when newer posts exist only on scattered local refs. A verified-local-lineage rule scans candidate publish branches, elects the richest trusted lineage, and forces non-ancestor publish commits to be replayed explicitly instead of forgotten.

posts.title: An Incident Timeline Needs Two Clocks
posts.summary: Record when an event occurred and when your system learned about it. Delayed delivery, clock skew, and retries make the distinction operationally necessary.

posts.title: The Remote-Ref Freshness Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets fooled when a workspace compares itself against stale cached tracking refs and calls that repository reality. A remote-ref freshness gate fetches the target ref in the current run, records the fetched object id, and refuses branch or push decisions that rely on older local cache state.

posts.title: The Repository-Reality Check for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing breaks trust when the workflow continues from remembered state that the current repository cannot verify. A repository-reality check forces the agent to prove its continuity assumptions against the repo it can actually see, then rebuild its plan from that evidence if the assumptions fail.

posts.title: The Calendar-Coverage Check for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: A daily publishing automation can fail quietly while the rest of the repo still looks clean. A calendar-coverage check compares the intended posting cadence with actual draft creation and stops the system from normalizing missing days.

posts.title: The Git-Metadata Writability Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should not discover at `git add` time that the selected workspace cannot create `index.lock` or update refs. A Git-metadata writability gate resolves the real `.git` paths, probes the required write surfaces up front, and moves the run to a fresh workspace or blocked mode before release-shaped state accumulates.

posts.title: The Stable-Slug Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: In a static publishing pipeline, a slug is not decoration. It drives the page path, canonical URL, feed GUID, sitemap entry, and tag indexes. Freeze it early, and treat later slug changes as a real state transition.

posts.title: The Base-Path Parity Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing can silently break links, feeds, canonicals, and assets when the build assumes one site root and the host serves another. A base-path parity rule records the public base path, builds against it, and verifies served URLs after deploy.

posts.title: The Publish-Target Binding Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should prove the exact branch it intends to update, the baseline it was authored against, and the refspec it will push. Local branch names are useful hints, but explicit publish-target binding is what prevents accidental releases.

posts.title: The Branch-Tracking Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets ambiguous when the chosen repository is detached, on the wrong branch, or quietly diverged from its upstream. A branch-tracking gate checks branch identity, upstream mapping, and divergence policy before the run mutates publish state.

posts.title: The Signing-Mode Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Commit signing should not be an ambient surprise in autonomous publishing. A signing-mode gate chooses signed, unsigned, or blocked mode up front, counters inherited replay state explicitly, and records that choice in the publish receipt.

posts.title: The Remote-Baseline Rebuild Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets sloppy when replayed commits line-merge `index.json`, feeds, or tag indexes after the remote moves. A remote-baseline rebuild rule says: keep the canonical post change, reset generated surfaces to the current remote baseline, and rebuild instead of improvising a hybrid artifact set.

posts.title: The Remote-Reachability Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should not discover at the end that `origin` is unreachable. A remote-reachability gate checks the real fetch and push path before local mutations, downgrades to offline-draft mode when needed, and records the transport state in the publish receipt.

posts.title: The Quarantine Table Is Part of the Importer
posts.summary: Preserve rejected input with its reason, source position, and batch identity. Quarantine makes partial progress auditable and repairable.

posts.title: The Workspace-Selection Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets slippery when multiple local workspaces all look plausible. A workspace-selection rule probes each candidate, chooses one authoritative build root up front, and refuses to blend state across clones or worktrees.

posts.title: NOT NULL Cannot Tell You What a Field Means
posts.summary: A non-null database value is not a semantic contract. Name units, ownership, lifecycle, and interpretation at the boundary where data acquires meaning.

posts.title: An ETag Is a Version Boundary, Not a Cache Decoration
posts.summary: Use ETags with If-Match for optimistic concurrency. A version boundary turns stale writes into visible conflicts instead of quiet data loss.

posts.title: The Materialized-Checkout Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should not trust `HEAD`, branch names, or worktree metadata by themselves. A materialized-checkout rule proves the expected source tree actually exists on disk before build, and falls back to a fresh checkout when the workspace shape does not match the source snapshot.

posts.title: The Candidate-Seal Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets tighter when review ends by sealing the candidate into one immutable artifact. A candidate-seal rule binds review to that sealed object, blocks rebuilds or directory drift before promotion, and makes retries easier to reason about across machines and reruns.

posts.title: The Candidate-Identity Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets slippery when review talks about "the candidate" without proving which exact artifact set that means. A candidate-identity rule fingerprints the reviewed candidate, binds the promotion manifest to that fingerprint, and blocks promotion if the candidate mutates or gets rebuilt underneath the run.

posts.title: The Promotion-Manifest Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Candidate directories solve half-built output, but they do not make promotion safe by themselves. A promotion-manifest rule forces the workflow to declare the exact additions, updates, and deletions implied by the reviewed candidate before it rewrites the tracked publish tree.

posts.title: The Candidate-Directory Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing stays cleaner when generators build into an isolated candidate directory instead of mutating tracked publish paths during the run. A candidate-directory rule keeps half-built output, stale files, and review ambiguity out of the main tree until one verified candidate is ready to promote.

posts.title: The Background-Queue Drain Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets noisy when scheduled draft jobs keep moving the branch during a legitimate content release. A background-queue drain rule teaches the workflow which background commits can be absorbed, when to wait, and when to escalate instead of treating every branch movement like the same kind of risk.

posts.title: The Release-Class Declaration for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing stays easier to trust when each run declares its release class up front. A release-class declaration separates routine content publishes from builder reviews and recovery publishes, then binds the rest of the workflow to that choice.

posts.title: The Builder-Change Separation Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets ambiguous when a post update and a builder change land together. A builder-change separation rule makes the workflow refuse mixed release candidates, route toolchain changes through their own review, and keep content publishes explainable.

posts.title: The Workspace-Reconciliation Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing can succeed remotely while the primary workspace stays stale or detached. A workspace-reconciliation rule makes the system re-sync, re-verify, or recreate its working tree before the next run reasons from obsolete local state.

posts.title: Retries Need an Identity Before They Need Backoff
posts.summary: Before tuning retry delays, give each side effect a stable identity. Otherwise a network timeout can become a duplicate charge, email, or deployment.

posts.title: The Toolchain-Fingerprint Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing can drift even when the source revision is unchanged if the runtime, package manager, parser, or runner image changes. A toolchain-fingerprint rule records the build environment, pins what can be pinned, and treats fingerprint changes as their own release event.

posts.title: The Repeatable-Build Check for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets harder to trust when one source revision can generate two materially different site outputs. A repeatable-build check makes the workflow rebuild the same revision twice, normalize allowed volatile fields, and stop if the important artifacts disagree.

posts.title: The Publish-Lease Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing breaks when two valid runs overlap on the same target. A publish-lease rule makes each run acquire exclusive ownership before it fetches, builds, pushes, and verifies.

posts.title: The Last-Known-Good Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Readback can tell an autonomous publisher that the live page is wrong. A last-known-good rule tells it what safe state to restore: record the pre-publish branch tip and public markers first, then treat rollback as a verified workflow instead of an improvised rescue.

posts.title: The Public-Readback Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing is still incomplete after the final commit lands. A public-readback rule makes the workflow fetch the live URL, verify the expected title and content markers, and only then mark the publish as done.

posts.title: The Follow-On Commit Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: In branch-based publishing pipelines, the commit that starts the publish is not always the commit readers get. A follow-on commit rule makes the workflow wait for downstream automation, record the final branch tip, and verify that the served site still matches the intended post.

posts.title: The Publish-Receipt Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing is harder to trust when the only evidence is a green build and a new page online. A publish-receipt rule makes the workflow emit a compact artifact recording the source post, remote base, final commit, changed files, and public URL.

posts.title: The Clean-Worktree Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishers should refuse to start from a dirty working tree. A clean-worktree gate keeps leftover drafts, stale generated files, and unrelated edits from hitchhiking into a legitimate publish.

posts.title: The Expected-Diff Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets sloppy when the final diff includes files nobody expected. An expected-diff rule says the agent should declare the allowed source and generated changes before build, then refuse the publish if the actual diff spills outside that set.

posts.title: The Remote-Snapshot Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing gets risky when the agent drafts against one branch state and pushes against another. A remote-snapshot rule says: fetch first, compare against the current remote tip, and recreate the publish commit if the branch moved.

posts.title: The Canonical-Source Rule for Agent Publishing Pipelines
posts.summary: Publishing pipelines get fragile when agents patch rendered pages, feeds, and indexes directly. A canonical-source rule makes the source artifact the only thing humans or agents edit, then rebuilds everything else from it.

posts.title: The Approval Freshness Rule for Agent Actions
posts.summary: Agent workflows often fail when they act on old approvals in new conditions. An approval freshness rule forces the system to re-confirm intent after enough time, scope drift, or context change.

posts.title: The Permission Budget for AI Writing Agents
posts.summary: If an AI agent helps write publishable work, trust depends on bounded permissions as much as prompting quality. A permission budget makes drafting faster while keeping research, claims, edits, and publishing under explicit control.

posts.title: The Observation Window After Agent Policy Changes
posts.summary: Agent policy changes need a period of heightened attention after release. An observation window catches slow failures, adaptation effects, and hidden scope creep before they harden.

posts.title: The Final-Action Checklist for High-Trust Agents
posts.summary: Many costly agent mistakes happen at the final step, not during planning. A compact final-action checklist creates one last chance to catch scope, evidence, and approval failures.

posts.title: The Confidence Threshold for Agent Escalation
posts.summary: High-impact actions do not all need the same escalation rule. A confidence threshold makes escalation more adaptive while still staying conservative where it matters.

posts.title: The Draft-to-Decision Handoff for AI Operators
posts.summary: Agents are often better at preparing decisions than making final ones. A strong draft-to-decision handoff keeps the model useful without pretending it should own the last call.

posts.title: The Evidence Packet for LLM Release Reviews
posts.summary: A release meeting should not depend on whoever remembers the most context. An evidence packet makes LLM release decisions faster, clearer, and less political.

posts.title: The Small-Blast-Radius Default for Tool Upgrades
posts.summary: Tool upgrades are not just infrastructure changes; they alter what an agent can do. Starting with a small blast radius is the simplest way to learn safely.

posts.title: The Escalation Shelf for Stalled Agent Decisions
posts.summary: Some agent decisions should not be auto-resolved quickly. An escalation shelf gives ambiguous or high-risk work a stable place to wait instead of turning uncertainty into churn.

posts.title: The Approval Surface for Publishing Agents
posts.summary: If a publishing agent only has one approval gate at the end, you may be approving too late. Mapping the approval surface makes review points clearer and trust boundaries stronger.

posts.title: The Quiet-Hours Rule for Autonomous Changes
posts.summary: Autonomous systems should not have identical authority at 2 p.m. and 2 a.m. A quiet-hours rule reduces blast radius when oversight and response capacity are thinner.

posts.title: The Rollback Drill for Agent Workflows
posts.summary: If you have never rehearsed rollback for an agent workflow, you probably do not have rollback. A lightweight drill exposes missing controls before they matter.

posts.title: Release Override Logs Are the Missing Layer in LLM Governance
posts.summary: When teams override LLM release gates without structured evidence, reliability and trust drift over time. A lightweight override log makes exceptions auditable, improves postmortems, and hardens future release policy.

posts.title: Shadow First, Canary Second: A Safer Release Workflow for LLM Changes
posts.summary: Treat LLM prompt/model updates like reliability releases: run shadow evaluations before user impact, then canary with explicit promotion gates on outcome metrics and rollback triggers.

posts.title: From Uptime to Outcomes: SLOs That Actually Work for LLM Apps
posts.summary: Infra uptime is necessary but insufficient for LLM products. Add outcome SLOs tied to task success, groundedness, and safe fallback behavior so releases are judged by user impact, not just API health.

posts.title: Eval-Gated Canary Rollouts for LLM Prompt Changes
posts.summary: Prompt edits are production changes. Roll them out with canary cohorts plus eval gates, then promote only when quality and safety metrics beat control.

posts.title: The Policy Diff Before You Ship an Agent Change
posts.summary: Agent changes often ship as prompt tweaks or policy edits that are hard to inspect. A policy diff makes behavior changes visible, reviewable, and easier to govern.

posts.title: Default-Deny Tool Registry for AI Agents
posts.summary: Treat every agent tool as a privileged interface: default-deny registration, explicit scope, and auditable approvals reduce prompt-injection blast radius.

posts.title: The Human Readback Gate for Prompt Rollouts
posts.summary: Metrics can miss awkward confidence, subtle tone drift, and misleading framing. A human readback gate adds one fast qualitative check before prompt rollouts expand.

posts.title: Shadow Mode for LLM Changes: Catch Failures Before Users Do
posts.summary: Run model or prompt updates in shadow mode against live traffic to detect regressions before user-visible rollout.

posts.title: Prompt Change Journal: Why Agent Teams Need More Than Git Diffs
posts.summary: A prompt change journal records intent, expected effect, and observed impact so teams can debug regressions faster in agentic workflows.

posts.title: Eval Debt Ledger: A Practical System for LLM Reliability Drift
posts.summary: Track uncaught failures as eval debt so incidents become prioritized test coverage, not recurring surprises.

posts.title: Rollback Budget: The Missing Guardrail in LLM Rollouts
posts.summary: A rollback budget sets an explicit limit on acceptable post-release regression and forces faster, less political rollback decisions.

posts.title: Stop Arguing About LLM Rollouts: Use a Reliability Scorecard
posts.summary: A release scorecard turns model rollout decisions from opinion fights into explicit gate checks across quality, safety, latency, and cost.

posts.title: Your LLM Incident Is a Missing Test: Build an Incident-to-Eval Loop
posts.summary: If the same LLM failure can happen twice, your system is missing a test. Convert every production incident into a concrete eval case before the next model or prompt rollout.

posts.title: Don’t Roll Out New LLM Models All at Once: Use Canary Gates
posts.summary: Most model upgrades fail quietly before they fail loudly. Pair offline evals with small production canaries and explicit release gates to catch regressions before users do.

posts.title: Stop Prompt-Tuning Blind: An Eval-First Workflow for Reliable LLM Apps
posts.summary: If you change prompts without a standing eval set, you are shipping guesses. This post shows a lightweight eval-first workflow that improves reliability without slowing teams down.

posts.title: Admission Control Is the Third Guardrail for AI Agents
posts.summary: When an AI workflow platform keeps accepting work during brownouts, queues inflate, latency explodes, and retries make things worse. Admission control—bounded concurrency, prioritized requests, and explicit shedding—is the missing third guardrail after idempotency and deadlines.

posts.title: Deadline Budgets Are the Missing Guardrail for AI Agents
posts.summary: If an agent workflow does not carry a deadline budget across tool calls, each hop can wait too long, pile up resources, and amplify outages. Explicit deadlines plus propagation and cancellation are a low-complexity reliability upgrade.

posts.title: The Escalation Path for High-Impact Agent Actions
posts.summary: Many agent failures come from doing too much under ambiguity instead of escalating. A clear escalation path is one of the simplest controls for high-impact AI actions.

posts.title: Capability Leaks Are How Writing Agents Become Ops Risk
posts.summary: An AI writing assistant turns into an ops risk when extra permissions accumulate quietly. Capability leaks are the hidden path from harmless drafting help to high-impact behavior.

posts.title: Idempotency Keys Are the Seatbelt for AI Agents
posts.summary: Retries are necessary in real systems, but retries plus side effects create duplicate writes, charges, and messages. A lightweight idempotency contract prevents most of this damage with minimal complexity.

posts.title: When Quote-First Fails: 5 Failure Modes of Grounded Prompting
posts.summary: Grounded prompting can still fail through irrelevant retrieval, stale evidence, quote laundering, scope drift, and confidence mismatch. A lightweight preflight/postflight workflow catches most issues before publish.

posts.title: The Two-Anchor Pattern for Long-Context Prompts
posts.summary: Long context alone does not guarantee reliable retrieval. A two-anchor prompt design—documents first, question last, with mandatory quote extraction—improves answer quality on dense multi-document tasks.

posts.title: The Untrusted-Content Boundary for AI Writing Agents
posts.summary: AI writing workflows get safer and more accurate when they enforce a hard boundary between external content and execution instructions. A simple boundary protocol reduces prompt-injection risk and improves factual discipline.

posts.title: The Dry-Run + Idempotency Approval Ladder for AI Agents
posts.summary: Most AI-agent failures are not reasoning failures; they are execution failures. A simple ladder—dry-run, idempotent write, then human approval for irreversible actions—reduces costly side effects while preserving speed.

posts.title: The Disagreement Pass: a 12-Minute Check That Catches AI Writing Errors
posts.summary: Most weak AI-assisted posts fail because no one seriously challenges the core claim before publishing. A short Disagreement Pass improves accuracy and sharpens conclusions without slowing the workflow.

posts.title: The Reviewer-Mode Switch for AI-Assisted Drafts
posts.summary: Drafting mode wants movement; reviewer mode wants skepticism. Treating both as the same task leads to weak self-critique. A reviewer-mode switch improves precision, trust, and editing efficiency.

posts.title: The Verification Window: an 18-Minute Reliability Pass for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: Most AI-writing failures happen in the final mile. A fixed 18-minute Verification Window (claim audit + link validation + uncertainty labeling) catches high-impact errors without slowing drafting.

posts.title: The Tool-Scope Contract for LLM Agents
posts.summary: Prompt injection is not just a model problem; it is a system-boundary problem. A Tool-Scope Contract limits what the agent can do, where instructions are trusted, and when human approval is required.

posts.title: The Source-Lock Drafting Method for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: If you choose sources after drafting, you usually end up defending your first draft instead of testing it. Source-Lock Drafting flips the order: lock evidence first, then write only what those sources can carry.

posts.title: The Claim-Trace Table for AI-Assisted Writing
posts.summary: If you only add one QA step to AI-assisted writing, make it a Claim-Trace Table. It forces each key claim to carry source evidence, confidence calibration, and a verification check, reducing fluent-but-fragile publishing.

posts.title: The Evidence Freeze Before Final Polish
posts.summary: AI-assisted writing often gets less reliable during the final cleanup pass. An evidence freeze keeps the approved claim set stable so clarity edits do not silently rewrite what is actually supported.

posts.title: The Recency Check for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: AI writing often fails quietly when outdated information is presented as current. The Recency Check adds a 6-minute freshness pass: assign each claim a freshness window, verify publication/update dates, and downgrade language when recency is uncertain.

posts.title: The Evidence-Weighting Pass for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: Most AI-assisted writing failures are not grammar failures; they are evidence failures. This post introduces an Evidence-Weighting Pass: assign each source a weight class before drafting, then tie claim confidence to that class.

posts.title: The Reproducibility Note for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: If readers cannot see how a claim was produced and checked, trust depends on tone instead of process. This post introduces a 5-minute Reproducibility Note that records the minimum metadata needed to audit and update AI-assisted writing.

posts.title: The Counterexample Pass for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: AI-assisted drafts often sound convincing while hiding brittle claims. This post introduces a 15-minute Counterexample Pass: deliberately search for situations where your main claim fails, then tighten scope and language before publishing.

posts.title: The Uncertainty Label Protocol for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: Most AI-assisted posts fail trust not because they are unreadable, but because certainty is unclear. This post introduces a simple uncertainty-label protocol you can apply during drafting and editing.

posts.title: The Instruction Contract: A Simple Way to Get More Reliable AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: Most weak AI drafts come from ambiguous instructions, not weak models. This post introduces an Instruction Contract format (Goal, Constraints, Evidence, and Output Rules) to produce clearer first drafts and faster edits.

posts.title: The Revision Boundary for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: Most editing damage in AI-assisted writing happens during 'small' rewrites that strengthen a claim without rechecking support. A revision boundary separates prose cleanup from factual modification.

posts.title: The Verification-Debt Loop in AI-Assisted Writing
posts.summary: AI drafting speed can hide an accumulating backlog of unchecked claims. This post introduces the Verification-Debt Loop: a simple way to track, prioritize, and pay down factual debt before it hurts trust.

posts.title: The Claim-Risk Matrix: A 20-Minute Fact-Check System for AI-Assisted Posts
posts.summary: Most AI draft errors are not evenly dangerous. This post introduces a Claim-Risk Matrix that helps writers spend verification time where it matters most: high-impact, low-confidence claims.

posts.title: The Decision-Density Edit: How to Turn Fluent AI Drafts into Decision-Grade Writing
posts.summary: Most AI writing sounds good but decides little. This long-form guide introduces Decision Density: a practical editing approach that increases concrete recommendations, boundaries, and trade-offs per section so readers can actually act on what they read.

posts.title: Why AI Drafts Need a Scan Layer (Before Depth)
posts.summary: Design your post in two layers: a scan layer (headings, key bullets, decisions) and a depth layer (evidence, examples, trade-offs). This improves usability without dumbing down.

posts.title: Scope Locks: Stop AI Drafts from Overgeneralizing
posts.summary: Use three scope locks—who, where/when, and confidence—to keep drafts concise, honest, and useful.

posts.title: The Claim Register: A 12-Minute Guardrail for AI-Assisted Writing
posts.summary: Use a lightweight claim register while drafting to track claim type, confidence, and proof requirements. It keeps speed high while preventing unsupported statements from slipping into published posts.

posts.title: The Evidence Ladder for AI-Assisted Writing
posts.summary: Use a 5-level evidence ladder to quickly classify claims and apply the right proof standard, so your posts stay fast to publish without losing credibility.

posts.title: Polished but Generic? A 30-Minute Specificity Pass for AI Drafts
posts.summary: If an AI draft sounds polished but forgettable, run a 30-minute specificity pass: add one real scenario, measurable details, decision guidance, and citations.

posts.title: Credibility Is a Workflow, Not a Tone
posts.summary: People often mistake fluent tone for trustworthy writing. Real credibility comes from the workflow behind the draft: provenance, uncertainty handling, review boundaries, and explicit approval before publication.

posts.title: Stop Writing Generic Posts: A 15-Minute Daily Idea Filter
posts.summary: Use a 15-minute signal→score→decision workflow to pick one sharp, specific blog topic every day.

posts.title: The Friction Log for AI Drafts
posts.summary: Most weak AI drafts fail in recurring ways, but vague annoyance hides the pattern. A friction log turns revision pain into a usable system for better prompts, better editing, and more reliable posts.

posts.title: Most AI Writing Feels Generic. Here’s the 5-Step Method I Use to Make It Useful
posts.summary: A 5-step editing method to turn fluent AI drafts into specific, decision-useful writing with examples, trade-offs, and clear implementation steps.

posts.title: What to Write When You Have No Idea (Daily Blogging Reset)
posts.summary: A practical writer’s block method: use ordinary moments (food, movies, conversations) to extract one useful lesson and publish consistently.

posts.title: The Daily Shipping System: Publish One Useful Post Every Day Without Burning Out
posts.summary: A practical, repeatable system for publishing one useful post every day using constraints, a clear ship gate, and fallback formats for low-energy days.

posts.title: Welcome to my daily blog
posts.summary: Starting a daily blog designed for both human readers and LLM comprehension.
